job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817, Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act (as amended October 6)

Items are in bill order. I reviewed only the text you provided, so some issues may already be addressed in the sponsors' offices or in report language.

1. **§2(1)(A), tonnage threshold.** The "by a single vessel" language lets an operator split a project across several vessels, each under 10,000 metric tons or 5,000 gross tons, and fall outside the definition. The threshold should aggregate all vessels and activities under common ownership, control, or a single license.

2. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "per year."** The bill doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry weight, whether it counts only nodules or all material lifted (including sediment returned to the sea), or whether "year" means calendar year, license year, or a rolling 12 months. A collector that lifts large volumes and discharges most of them could argue it falls below the threshold.

3. **§2(1)(A), mineral scope.** "Polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources" leaves cobalt-rich crusts and seafloor massive sulfides unclear. Define "seabed mineral resources" to cover all seabed minerals so non-nodule operations can't be argued out of scope.

4. **§2(1)(A), depth floor.** Confirm the 200-meter floor is intentional. It also doesn't say how depth is measured at the point of recovery.

5. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** The bill never defines which Secretary is meant. §6 refers to the Secretary of State and §4 to NOAA, so this provision could be read as referring to a different official.

6. **§2(1)(B), comparability determination.** The Secretary's power to find activities "comparable" has no criteria, procedure, notice, deadline, or judicial review. The catch-all could be used to clear specific projects, or the Secretary could simply never act on it. The comparison is also odd: it measures ecological risk against a volume threshold.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and corporations organized under federal law or in D.C. and the territories. It is also easy to evade by incorporating abroad or using foreign subsidiaries of U.S. parents. Add a control or beneficial-ownership test.

8. **Throughout, "person" is undefined.** The term appears in §3(a) and §5 but is defined nowhere. Add a definition that covers corporations, partnerships, LLCs, government entities, and officers and directors.

9. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** "Equipped for the recovery" is undefined, so a vessel that is designed or converted for collection but not yet fitted, or that uses detachable collection gear, may escape. The definition also doesn't say whether it reaches foreign-flagged vessels.

10. **§3(a), "engage in."** The phrase doesn't clearly reach financing, insurance, chartering, equipment manufacture, vessel services, processing, transport, or the sale and import of minerals from commercial deep-seabed mining. A ban limited to recovery leaves a market for minerals mined elsewhere. Add explicit bans on importing, selling, and processing such minerals, and on knowingly financing or supporting covered activity.

11. **§3(a), territorial reach.** "In the United States" isn't defined, so it's unclear whether it includes the Exclusive Economic Zone and continental shelf. Foreign persons and foreign-flagged vessels mining in areas under U.S. jurisdiction, or in the Area beyond national jurisdiction, may fall outside the prohibition.

12. **§3(b), grandfathered exploration licenses.** Exploration licenses are not commercial recovery permits, but the text would let commercial recovery continue under a license originally issued for exploration. Limit the exemption to exploration below the threshold and require that any grandfathered license be registered and listed.

13. **§3(b), cutoff date.** Keying the exemption to "the date of enactment" invites a rush to license during the 180-day gap and possibly before enactment. Add a cutoff tied to introduction and a moratorium on new licenses, permits, and approvals.

14. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** The exemption has no cap on tonnage, duration, or sale of recovered material, and it requires no approved plan, notice, or reporting. Operators could label commercial extraction as "environmental assessment." Require prior Secretary approval of an assessment plan, a tonnage cap well below the threshold, a bar on selling or exporting material beyond test samples, and reporting.

15. **§4, scope of registry and reports.** Registration and reporting apply only to covered vessels, so operations below 5,000 gross tons, and any activity exempted under §3(b) or §3(c), go unreported. Extend reporting to all activity that is exempted or below the threshold.

16. **§4(b), report content.** "Describing the recovery activities" doesn't specify what must be reported. Require tonnage, location, depth, sediment discharge and plume data, equipment, and the legal basis for any exemption, with public availability.

17. **§4, "operator" and "certified."** Neither term is defined, so an owner, charterer, or lessee could each argue it isn't the operator. The standard for certification is also undefined. Define the term, impose joint liability, and set a certification standard that carries personal liability for false statements.

18. **§4, no deadlines, verification, or inspection.** The bill sets no registration deadline, no audit or verification mechanism, and no right of inspection or records access. Add these.

19. **§5, penalties don't reach §4.** Civil and criminal penalties attach only to violations of §3, so failure to register, failure to report, or filing a false report carries no penalty under the Act. Add penalties for §4 violations.

20. **§5, no enforcement authority or procedure.** The bill doesn't designate an enforcing agency or say who brings civil actions, whether penalties are assessed administratively or judicially, what the limitations period is, or what funding supports enforcement. Name the enforcing agency and give it inspection, boarding, subpoena, and penalty-assessment authority.

21. **§5(a), remedies limited to fines.** There is no injunctive relief, no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals, and no disgorgement of profits. A company earning large revenues may treat $1 million per day as a cost of doing business. The bill also doesn't say how "each day" is counted for continuing violations.

22. **§5(a), timing conflict.** The penalty applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 makes the Act effective 180 days later. Align the penalty date with the effective date.

23. **§5, no citizen suit or whistleblower provision.** Without these, enforcement depends entirely on agency action. Consider a citizen-suit provision and whistleblower protections.

24. **§5(b), criminal provisions.** "Willfully" is undefined. The bill has no provisions for aiding and abetting, conspiracy, or attempt, and no liability for officers or directors who direct violations. It also doesn't address false certifications under §4(b).

25. **§6, international agreement.** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no obligation to conclude an agreement, requires no report to Congress, and sets no consequence for failure. It's also unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to starting or concluding talks, and "equivalent to those in section 3" is undefined. Add a reporting requirement and a review trigger.

26. **§7(a), joint-resolution trigger.** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the bill doesn't require that the National Academies be tasked or set a deadline for its report. It's also unclear whether "can be conducted" refers to technology or to practice. Without a trigger, the exit route may never be used; with one, the standard will be contested. Define the standard and set a deadline for the report.

27. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), direct conflict.** §7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until a joint resolution is enacted, but §7(b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment, with no resolution required. The sunset would end the prohibition and all penalties on schedule, regardless of scientific findings. This is the most serious problem in the bill. Delete the sunset or make it conditional.

28. **§7(b), no savings clause.** Even if the sunset stays, the bill doesn't preserve liability for violations committed before expiration, pending enforcement actions, or reports already due. The general repeal rule may not reliably cover a sunset. Add an explicit savings clause.

29. **§8 and §3(b), effective date gap.** The prohibition takes effect 180 days after enactment, while §3(b) and §5(a) key off the enactment date. Depending on the reading, operations may continue without penalty during that window, and the licensing rush in item 13 becomes possible. Make the prohibition, penalties, and grandfathering rules take effect on the same date, with an interim moratorium.

30. **Whole Act, missing general provisions.** The bill has no severability clause, no statement on preemption or preservation of state authority (which invites challenge over state waters), no rulemaking authority, no judicial review provision, and no appropriation. Add these.

31. **Whole Act, international exposure.** The bill doesn't address U.S. persons who hold International Seabed Authority contracts or sponsor foreign contractors, which creates litigation risk and may be the first argument opponents raise. This is partly a policy question, not just drafting.

---

**Top priorities before Thursday:**

1. **Fix the §7(a)/§7(b) conflict** (item 27). This is the most damaging problem and the easiest for opponents to exploit.
2. **Close the §3(c) environmental-assessment exemption** (item 14) and tighten **§3(b)** (items 12–13).
3. **Fix the aggregation and definitions in §2** (items 1, 7, 10) so the prohibition can't be split, reflagged, or financed around.
4. **Designate an enforcing agency and penalty procedure** and extend penalties to §4 (items 19–21).
5. **Resolve the effective-date gap** (items 22, 29).

I'm not a lawyer, and this is a policy and drafting review rather than a legal opinion. Before the markup, have Senate Legislative Counsel or the Coalition's counsel check the proposed fixes, and confirm with the sponsors' offices whether any of these issues are already handled in the manager's amendment or planned report language.
